items.title: Territorial Acknowledgement
notes: Mayor McCabe opened the meeting with the following Territorial Acknowledgement:

We would like to begin by acknowledging that the land on which we gather (land on which we are broadcasting from) today is the land traditionally cared for by the Haudenosaunee, Anishinaabe and Chonnontan People. We also acknowledge the enduring presence and deep traditional knowledge and philosophies of the Indigenous People with whom we share this land today.

items.title: Moment of Reflection
notes: Mayor McCabe provided Council with a moment of reflection.
At the beginning of this Council meeting, we pause to think about the needs of our community. May we show wisdom and compassion in all our decisions.

It was almost a year ago in June that Martin Powless, Knowledge Keeper and Wampum Belt Maker, and Rita VanEvery presented three replica Wampum belts commissioned by the City - the Hiawatha Wampum, the Two-Row Wampum and the Dish with One Spoon Wampum.

These belts are a physical representation of the oral history of treaties and settlement of the area around the Great Lakes Region extending along a portion of the St. Lawrence River. These are significant representations of our colonial history and are still seen to this day as a reminder to all of us of the responsibilities we hold as treaty people.

We have learned that Martin passed last week and extend the condolences to his friends and family, we thank him for these pieces which we display to remind the public, staff and Council of our commitment towards reconciliation.
Tonight we will receive additional training and information from Six Nations and thank them for their attendance.

items.title: Six Nations Education and Training Workshop
notes: Phil Monture, Land Rights Consultant, Six Nations spoke about his experience as a Land Rights Consultant over the last 50 years. He explained the significance of the different treaties entered into by the Five Nations with the settlers.

He spoke about the treaty that governs the Haldimand Tract and the six miles of land on either side of the Grand River, and how the Six Nations have less than 5% of the land promised to them. He specifically described Block 2, where Waterloo is located, and the history surrounding the dissecting of the Haldimand Tract.

Daylon Gee, Land Use Technician, Lands and Resources Office, Six Nations spoke about the legal duty to consult. He described the treaty rights more fully, including the rights to land, rights to occupy, government rights, cultural and societal rights. He spoke about the rules for consultation under the Planning Act, and stated that new Bills being passed by the province to get homes built faster often undermine the rights of the First Nations who live in these areas.

Daylon Gee discussed the conditions on the Six Nations reserves, such as water contamination and poor road conditions, and stressed the importance of Indigenous consultations. Consultations ensure the protection of treaty rights and the Indigenous way of life, build relationships and trust with the communities, and it’s the law. Some of the ways that communities can be accommodated include financial settlements, equity partnerships, joint land stewardship, job opportunities, and education opportunities. He mentioned a consultation package for working with the Region that is being developed.

Lauren Jones, Wildlife and Stewardship Manager, Six Nations, spoke about her role within the Consultation and Accommodation Process (CAP) Team providing environmentally specific comments. She described processes and frameworks they have to follow as stagnated and not made with the intentions of including Indigenous viewpoints. She spoke about the connection between the natural environment and the identities of the Indigenous people within Ontario, and how it differs from Western, settler perspectives.

She continued to say that disruptions to the natural environment directly affect Indigenous communities on multiple levels, with pollution and degradation disrupting their way of life and leading to food insecurity. The Wildlife and Stewardship Office tends to push for going above and beyond the minimum that is set out in frameworks, for improvements to the environment, not just replacing what was taken, and advocating for the protection of species important to Indigenous cultures, which may not be on any endangered species lists.
Phil Monture added that he wants to work with Council and the municipalities as allies, and work through differences. He expressed that he wants to build on relationships with open communication.
Ron Ormson and Joel Cotter responded to questions of Council. Daylon Gee also responded to questions of Council.

notes: Response Plan
Report No.: CORP2025-022
Prepared By: Tracie Bell, Justin McFadden, Paul Hettinga, Francis Reyes

Filipa Reynolds, Tracie Bell, Francis Reyes, Paul Hettinga, Justin McFadden and Jeyas Balaskanthan, Executive Director, Uptown Waterloo Business Improvement Area (BIA) gave a presentation outlining the City’s response to the US tariffs. Francis Reyes spoke about the desire to streamline the development approval process, and the need to collaborate with area municipalities on capital projects. Paul Hettinga outlined the different areas of advocacy the City is engaging with, including grants, and the extension of the tax deferral program. Justin McFadden spoke about the support for start-ups in the Region with the Accelerator Centre, as well as the resources the City is offering for local businesses to support them. Jeyas Balaskanthan outlined the Uptown BIA’s response to the tariffs. He spoke about the concerns of the BIA members and the desire to continue to buy local.
Filipa Reynolds, Tracie Bell, Francis Reyes, Paul Hettinga and Justin McFadden responded to questions of Council.

Tanner Bergsma, Resident of Waterloo spoke about the need for the City to amend its procurement by-law to specifically include a lens of inclusion and equity, and highlight businesses that uplift marginalized members of the community. motions.text: WHEREAS the Province of Ontario’s Bill 17 – “Protect Ontario by Building Faster and Smarter” Act recently passed Second Reading and is now open for comment; and WHEREAS the City of Waterloo broadly supports provincial efforts to standardize and streamline development approvals to boost housing and economic growth; and WHEREAS the City of Waterloo was recently recognized as a top performing community under the Housing Accelerator Fund, having implemented numerous initiatives to increase the amount of affordable and attainable housing including; allowing four units and four storeys as of right city wide, increasing height in Major Transit Station Areas, expanding corridors, utilizing city owned land as part of a development at 2025 University Avenue among many other initiatives; and WHEREAS Bill 17, in part, aims to standardize the application of the Ontario Building Code by removing municipalities’ ability to set higher green building standards; and WHEREAS approximately 45% of all Waterloo Region community greenhouse gas emissions are from building emissions; and WHEREAS the City of Waterloo has a goal of reducing our community greenhouse gas emissions 50% by 2030 and to be net-zero by 2050; and WHEREAS WR Community Energy has been working on the creation and harmonization of High-Performance Development Standards since 2021, with the intention of implementation in 2026; and WHEREAS the implementation of High-Performance Development Standards is critical to achieve our community greenhouse gas emissions reduction goals; and WHEREAS High-Performance Development Standards are a planning tool for municipalities that respect the Ontario Building Code without sacrificing the important safety elements therein, do not require technical requirements over and above the Ontario Building Code, and are intended to complement the Ontario Building Code, not override it; and WHEREAS High-Performance Development Standards help ensure the long-term affordability of living in new homes by accounting for the long- term operating costs of energy, incentivizing lower carbon and lower cost sources of energy; and WHEREAS Waterloo Region is a leader in green building technologies in the construction industry and in related sectors; and WHEREAS High-Performance Development Standards create demand for specialized skills in green building technologies, leading to the creation of skilled job opportunities, and contributing to local economic prosperity; and WHEREAS High-Performance Development Standards are integral to ensure smart growth in Waterloo Region, affording predictability for local utilities, and ensuring long-term affordability by ensuring homes are built with higher efficiency of water usage, preserving our groundwater supply; and WHEREAS fifteen municipalities in Ontario have already implemented equivalent High-Performance Development Standards; and WHEREAS to meet local, provincial, and federal climate targets, all buildings that are built today in a GHG intensive manner are buildings that will need to be retrofitted in a costly manner in the near future to meet those goals; and WHEREAS the current Ontario Building Code falls short of the National Building Code when it comes to energy efficiency, necessitating municipal leadership to achieve local community goals. NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED: THAT the City of Waterloo advocates for elimination of provisions within Bill 17 that seek restricting local planning authority, particularly as pertains to High-Performance Development Standards; and THAT the City of Waterloo encourages the Province of Ontario to at minimum align the forthcoming Ontario Building Code with energy Tier 3 of the new National Building Code and/or adopt more stringent energy performance standards such as has been implemented in British Columbia and is contemplated in other Provinces such as Quebec; and THAT Council directs staff to provide holistic commentary on Bill 17 to the Environmental Registry of Ontario and in particular, related to concerns of restricting local planning authority for High-Performance Development Standards; and THAT Council directs staff to continue the work on community High- Performance Development Standards to guide future alternative pathways to strengthen and maintain High-Performance Development Standards in new home construction; AND THAT a copy of this resolution be sent to the Premier of Ontario, the Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing, to local and area MPPs, the Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO), the Ontario Big City Mayors (OBCM), the Association of Municipal Managers, Clerks and Treasurers of Ontario (AMCTO), and to the Region of Waterloo and local area municipalities.
